title: Obtain Capabilities: Digital Certificates
summary: This sub-technique covers buying or stealing an SSL/TLS certificate issued by a real certificate authority, so the resulting chain of trust validates on any normal client. It is the counterpart to developing a self-signed certificate: here the adversary does not run their own authority, they obtain trusted material from someone else. Purchase routes include front organisations and impersonation of a previously compromised entity, using stolen business records to satisfy identity validation. Theft routes include taking certificate and private key material from a compromised third party, or from a certificate authority itself, which historically has forced an authority out of business and required mass reissuance. Domain validation certificates are the cheapest path, because authorities issue them free once the applicant proves control of a domain, usually through a DNS record or a file on a web server. A newly registered or hijacked domain therefore becomes a trusted certificate in minutes. Adversaries use the result to encrypt command and control over web protocols, to give credential harvesting pages a padlock, or to support traffic interception if the certificate is installed in a victim trust store. Detection has to move past chain validity and look at the identity behind it: domain registration age, whether the organisation name matches the domain, duplicate serials or shared keys across unrelated hosts, and certificate transparency records. Legitimate services generally present certificates tied to a domain and organisation with a credible history.

beginner.definition: SSL and TLS certificates keep web traffic private and prove who owns a site. This technique is about attackers getting a real one, issued by a genuine certificate authority, by buying it or stealing it. The certificate then passes normal trust checks.
beginner.whyItMatters: A trusted certificate makes harmful infrastructure look normal. Users see a padlock and believe the site is safe. Attackers can even use stolen certificates to read traffic they should not see, which puts private data at risk.
howItWorks: The attacker registers a new domain or takes over an old one.
They then send a certificate request to a real, publicly trusted certificate authority.
They prove control of that domain, often with a special DNS record or a small file.
The authority then issues a valid certificate, sometimes at no cost at all.
They install it on their server so clients accept the connection without warnings.
Defenders spot it later through domain age, certificate logs, and shared keys.
beginner.example: A city issues parking permits to companies with premises. One applicant invents a company name and shows fake papers for an empty office. Another steals a permit from a real firm. Both permits check out at the roadside because the city really did print them. Only a closer look at who actually owns the permit reveals the problem.
takeaways: A valid certificate means an authority checked something, not that the owner is honest.
Free domain validated certificates make trusted looking infrastructure cheap.
Check domain age and certificate transparency logs, not just the padlock.

objectives: Explain how adversaries obtain legitimately issued certificates through purchase or theft.
Describe what a certificate authority checks before issuing a domain validated certificate.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from creating a self-signed certificate.
Explain why a valid chain of trust is not proof that a site is trustworthy.
Use certificate metadata such as domain age and shared keys to spot suspicious infrastructure.
